title: Nvidia's post-Jensen era kicks off with a bang
excerpt: Nvidia shared key info on an earnings call, reporting higher-than-expected revenue — and reiterating the company would continue on without Huang.
content_html:
Nvidia hits the ground running in post-Jensen era

By Dan DeFrancesco

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

Executive Editor and lead writer for BI Today

2026-11-18T11:48:21.667Z

Jensen who?

That was the vibe on Nvidia's earnings call last night as the AI giant looked to move on following longtime CEO Jensen Huang's shocking resignation less than a week ago.

"We've got this," said interim CEO Colette Kress, previously Nvidia's CFO, when closing out the call.

Investors seemed to agree, at least initially. The stock was trading up over 5% after hours.

In yesterday's newsletter, I outlined the big questions investors would want answered from Nvidia's leadership on the call. Here's how they did:

Is Jensen Huang actually gone? Yes, according to Harvey Jones, the chairman of Nvidia's board. He said the board "unanimously accepted" Huang's resignation and "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

But someone should tell Jensen Huang that. The former CEO is still angling for the job. With the "Stand with Jensen" movement in full swing, Huang broke his silence earlier on Tuesday to say he'd be "honored" to return to Nvidia if its board decides it's in the company's best interest. The internet was quick to react.

We didn't get more details than that from Nvidia, though. Jones said the company "will not be addressing or taking questions" about Huang's resignation and its investigation.

How's the CEO search going? Be patient. Jones said it's looking for a permanent fix "as quickly as possible," but it won't rush things until it finds "exactly the right person." And that "right person" could be inside or outside Nvidia, according to Jones.

There was one crucial clue about who the pick could be, according to BI's Geoff Weiss. When that potential successor joined the Q&A, they proceeded to say absolutely nothing. Not a word. BI's Alistair Barr breaks down why their appearance mattered.

If Nvidia's board is looking for help, one tech legend has some advice.

Will Nvidia's strategy change? This was perhaps the most nuanced answer of the group. Kress started the call saying the company's "roadmap is on track." Nvidia is also still supportive of an open AI ecosystem. That puts it opposite Anthropic, which is also a customer, in the ongoing debate about what's best for AI development.

Kress took a hard line on China, though. She said Nvidia is "no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China." That business accounted for $2.4 billion last quarter.

Closer to home, Nvidia's dealmaking spree might look slightly different in its Jensen-free era. Support for neoclouds will continue, but Kress said Nvidia would be "disciplined and selective." Nvidia wants companies to have their ducks in a row regarding capital and compute resources. Any delays or challenges to buildouts mean, "our guarantee doesn't exist anymore," Kress said.

Oh, and how did earnings go? Yes, let's not forget about the actual earnings. (You know, the reason we did this whole thing.) Nvidia's quarterly revenue ($115.8 billion), data-center revenue ($107.6 billion), and adjusted earnings per share ($2.68) beat estimates.

Q4 revenue guidance ($130.0 billion) was also above estimates. And Nvidia's more bullish on next year. Kress said Nvidia's expecting 75% growth next year, higher than its previous forecast of 70%.

Dan DeFrancesco
